synopsis: Auto-GCAS takes control of F-16 and F-35 aircraft to avert imminent ground collision; it is a precedent for automatic intervention, not object-triggered machine braking [f15732, f1446]. Research began in the early 1980s, F-16 Block 40/50 retrofits began in September 2014, and capability development took about three decades [f1439, f1440, f1461]. F-35 integration followed in 2019, with the manufacturer attributing delivery seven years ahead of plan to agile development and reuse; this illustrates fast reuse after slow foundational construction, not elimination of flight testing [f1443, f15742, f1445]. A 2007 NASA release reported 98 percent effectiveness, and Lockheed Martin credited the system with saving eight F-16 pilots by 2019, although the booklet identifies save counts as secondary-press evidence [f1442, f1444, f2023]. Nuisance-free operation and avoiding harm were explicit priorities, motivating the recommendation to prove a machine brake does no harm and does not annoy before proving protection [f1441, f15743]. Validation combined simulation and flight tests with nuisance criteria, and acceptance came from military bodies—the US Air Force and Joint Program Office—rather than a civil regulator [f1915, f1919, f15741].
